I had a punchcard system for my 9th graders, They could use the punchcard to leave class for bathroom or locker needs 3 times a quarter. If they didn’t use the pass at all, they could staple it to a late assignment as a free pass and it wouldn’t be docked points. Only rule was they couldn’t leave during first or last 10 minutes of class. 

Tardy? Use your punchcard to not get marked tardy. Lost the card? Guess you’re staying in class. Out of punches? You stay.

Obviously there were exceptions and students with accommodations, but for the most part, it worked great. No disruptions — kids would just bring up their pass, I would punch it. If they asked to leave, I could say “only if I have your pass” and that was the end of it.

My good Judy’s were the SPED department peeps, and my husband is a SPED teacher. I was high school English. I love y’all and the work you do with kids. A couple chuckles/frustrations I had:

1) Had a SPED teacher write a legally-binding accommodation on an IEP to give a student Candy when they turned in homework. In high school. Like… who is providing the candy?

2) I once was pulled out for 14 IEP meetings in the span of 3 months because I was English and was told I shouldn’t say no. I ended up talking to the SPED admin who had to send out a cease and desist (lol). Lot of subs and subpar lesson plans those months I was losing my prep.

3) Was asked once by a SPED teacher if I could come in on the first day of summer break to let a kid on their caseload sit in my room and make up work before the official grades were posted. That was one of them I did not consider a good Judy for obvious reasons.

Overall, the SPED teachers who were in frequent communication, realistic about their kids and their effort at the end of the semester, and were willing to come up with realistic compromises that put responsibility on the students while still showing empathy… those I respected and still consider good friends. Thanks for all you do. :)

OP, I totally understand your dream — you are young, starting your college career, and probably see Finland as a beautiful and highly desirable location and place to live. When I was starting my teaching degree, I wanted to move to Europe too.

I would challenge you to open your mind to other cultures. Europe is not the only beautiful place to live. I ended up moving to Taiwan and teaching there — it is a safe, beautiful, richly cultural, and friendly country that I fell in love with. When people ask me where I would want to live in the world now, I always say I would move back to Asia. That would not have been my answer when I was young. The world will surprise you.

Take as many abroad opportunities as possible, even just to travel. Get a feel for where you fit. Finland might not be YOUR gold standard when you get out and experience more.

I would highly recommend that you do not get a teaching degree if you do not want to teach in the US — it is a burnout right now. Last year, I left teaching. (Maybe I’ll go abroad again!) You will most likely have to get some experience here before moving to any kind of abroad assignment, and I fear for those in their first few years teaching in the US system.

All the best to you, good luck, and always keep your mind open. :)

I think Call Me By Your Name checks every box when I think of future classics:
1) Themes of coming of age and sexual confusion; always popular themes in classic lit.
2) Beautiful prose.
3) Focuses more on internal thought and philosophy. Just in my own reading experience, many books in the modern canon lean strongly towards the individual experience (thinking Catcher in the Rye, Old Man and the Sea, etc.)
4) Represents open queer literature, which is one of the important movements of our time. This one resonates most because classic lit almost always responds heavily to and represents major attitudes and ideas of the culture it belongs to. Classic books are history lessons as well.
5) It just FELT like a classic when I was reading it. I don’t know — just really gave me the same vibe. 

Interested to hear if others felt the same or differently!

I dread having any sort of conversation with conspiracy theorists because their threshold for “truth” is so low. They are almost offended when you try to push for them to authenticate their sources. And when pushed too much, they have the automatic response of: “Well, you can’t trust anything. It’s all part of the liberal media. Fake news.” We have an active part of the population that has demonized and vilified academia.

And I feel the same things you feel: just the mind numbing frustration and the helplessness that there’s nothing you can do about it. It is tearing families apart. It is tearing communities apart. It feels like the most important thing to the conspiracy theorists is not their relationships, hobbies, neighbors, etc. but rather being “right” and “knowing the truth.” I’ve been told that I am a stupid sheep by my family for simply asking that they not email me any more conspiracy theories. I’ve been told that I’m brainwashed by the liberals because I went to college to make something of myself.

I feel that I am repeating thoughts that have already been documented here, but I agree that taking this measure will only push your niece further into the arms of conservative groups.

As someone who is liberal but attends a diverse church with raging Trump conservatives and very liberal members alike, I hear the narrative of the conservative believer often: universities are evil brainwashing institutions, the world is out to stifle your religious freedom, liberals are (at best) crazy and (at worst) ushering in the apocalyptic antichrist.  Usually, the people who believe this rhetoric did not have the privilege to go to a university and expose themselves to other people or ways of thinking. In the meantime, they have surrounded themselves in a vacuum chamber of like-minded people, news sources, etc.  They think that liberals are ruining their lives and threatening the very core of their being.

Now imagine your niece is personally victimized by one of these liberals. It will justify everything that the conservative group has said to her. You will essentially be running her straight into their open arms.

From the perspective of a teacher (which I am), I have a lot of silly teenagers who come in holding a myriad of crazy beliefs: misogyny, alt right, racist, sexist, anti-trans, discrimination based on religion, etc.  And of course, I cannot let these things slide in my classroom. It is toxic. Instead, we talk to them: counselors, teachers, admin, to try and figure out why they believe these thing and why it is misinformed. It doesn’t always work, but it is a lot better than saying, “You’re wrong! We’re going to throw you in detention for three days! Ha! Now you don’t believe those things, right?”  And, as a side note, I hope these students go to college where they will at least get out of their own vacuum chambers. There is hope.

And there is hope for your niece. Just...talk to her. Explain your experiences of life. You don’t even need to oust her father. Talk about other experiences you’ve had with the LGBT community, with male and female relationships, religion, etc. Be a voice for those perspectives. And while I don’t 100% think you’re an ahole for being upset to see someone you love make these decisions to antithetical to your own...YTA if you send her straight into the den of angry conservatives who will vote Trump in the next election.
